text: {"thinking": "Competing explanations: (H1) Honest: no run exceeded 50,000 GPU-hours; records match third-party data. Check: utility_energy, inventory vs system_list, balance_checks. (H2) Honest but messy: lost logs, late payments, or periodic batch inference/cooling that looks like training. Check: log_escrow vs scheduler_log, power_spectrum on suspicious days, outbound_traffic. (H3) Split run: one training process labelled as several smaller jobs or customers, each under the threshold. Check: interconnect_tap on A-B link, customer_check on register entries, bank_payments to see who pays. (H4) Hidden hardware: GPUs or a cluster left off the system list running training. Check: inventory vs system_list, utility_energy vs listed load. (H5) Mislabelled run: training logged as inference, or low-communication training to dodge the tap. Check: chip_probe live, outbound_traffic (training sends little to the internet), power_spectrum. (H6) Retroactive log edits: check log_escrow vs scheduler_log. Plan: map systems first with inventory (third party) and system_list.", "action": "inventory", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Competing explanations: (H1) Honest: no run exceeded 50,000 GPU-hours; records consistent, messiness (lost logs, late payments) is innocent. (H2) Split run: one coordinated run labelled/billed as several jobs or customers (possibly via shell customers the operator controls), each under threshold but jointly above. Check: interconnect_tap on A-B and within clusters for cross-job traffic, customer_check register entries, bank_payments for common payers, scheduler/escrow consistency. (H3) Hidden hardware: GPUs not on the operator's system list or tap list running training. Check: inventory (manufacturer) vs system_list, utility_energy vs listed load, power_spectrum on feeds. (H4) Mislabelled workload: training labelled as batch inference or 'evaluation', or low-communication training disguised as inference. Check: chip_probe live, interconnect_tap rates (10 MB/s vs 10 kB/s), outbound_traffic (training sends little to internet), power spectrum lines. (H5) Edited records: scheduler log altered after the fact. Check: log_escrow vs scheduler_log. (H6) Innocent anomaly: periodic power line from cooling or batch inference, or late payments/missing logs, mistaken for violation. Check: corroborate any line with tap traffic and probe. Start by mapping systems: inventory (third-party) first, then system_list.", "action": "inventory", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Inventory, which the manufacturer vouches for, shows 2000 GPUs at the site in two serial blocks: 1200 and 800. That probably maps to cluster A and cluster B. Next I'll get the operator's system_list and compare it with these counts, to see whether any hardware is missing or unlisted (H4).", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Inventory (manufacturer) shows 2000 GPUs: SN100001-SN101200 (1200) and SN101201-SN102000 (800). Next, compare against the operator's system list to see whether every serial is listed and on the tap list.", "action": "system_list", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The system list matches the manufacturer's inventory: A has 1200 nodes (SN block of 1200) and B has 800 (SN block of 800), 2000 in total, so there's no sign of unlisted hardware yet. The scheduled-job pools are A-0501 to A-1200 (700 GPUs) and B-0401 to B-0800 (400 GPUs). The threshold is small next to these pools. 700 GPUs reach 50,000 GPU-hours in about 71 hours, so a multi-day run on the A pool could cross it. Next I'll get grid-vouched utility_energy for days 1-30. It shows the actual site load per day, which I can compare with logs and use to spot sustained flat high-power periods that suggest large training runs.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "The system list (A: 1200 nodes, B: 800 nodes) matches the manufacturer's 2000 GPUs by count, so there is no evidence of hidden hardware so far. Next I will get the operator's declared job record, then compare it against the sealed escrow and third-party sources.", "action": "scheduler_log", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "The scheduler log declares three jobs, all well under 50k GPU-hours: ft-0412 at 7,200, ft-0419 at 7,200 and bt-0423 at 9,600. This record is vouched for only by the operator. Kestrel Search's job is labelled batch, so H4 (mislabelled training) is possible. Each declared job also leaves large blocks of scheduled-job nodes and days idle on paper. Next I check the sealed escrow copies, which I control, to see whether the operator's log was edited after the fact (H5).", "action": "log_escrow", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Utility data shows a sustained flat high-load period on days 22-27, with partial load on day 28, on both F1 and F2. Its size fits most of the scheduled pools on A and B running near full power for about six days, which could exceed the threshold if it was one coordinated run. It could also be batch inference or separate customers' jobs. Next I'll get the sealed log escrow to see what the operator recorded at the time.", "action": "log_escrow", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The escrow matches the current log, so the log was not edited after the fact. That does not show the log is true, though: a run could have been left out or mislabelled on the day itself. Next I use a third-party source, the grid operator's energy record. The declared jobs plus the inference pools give a predictable baseline. Sustained excess load, especially on days with no declared job, would point to unlisted training (H2/H4). An energy profile that fits the declared jobs would support H1.", "action": "utility_energy", "args": {"first_day": 1, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "The escrow matches every day, so the logs weren't edited afterwards (rules out H6), though the entries could still have been false when written. My estimate from grid data: in days 22-27, F1 rose about 10.9 MWh/day (about 454 kW, roughly 700 GPUs going from idle to training) and F2 about 6.2 MWh/day (about 258 kW, roughly 400 GPUs). That is about the full scheduled pools of A and B for about 6 days. A single run that size would be well over 50,000 GPU-hours; even the A pool alone would be about 100k. Next I'll see what the operator recorded for those GPUs (jobs, customers, job types) in days 20-30.", "action": "scheduler_log", "args": {"first_day": 20, "last_day": 30}}

{"thinking": "The previous reply was cut off by a safety classifier, so I am not repeating it. I am moving on with a short next step. The grid energy record only shows step changes on the declared job days, so a hidden run would have to be steady in the background. Today is a live audit day, and my own tap on cluster A will show whether there is training-level traffic between GPUs now.", "action": "interconnect_tap", "args": {"link": "A", "day": 27}}

{"thinking": "The A-B tap on day 24 reads about 218 GB/s across the clusters. If the A jobs and the B jobs were unrelated, cross-cluster traffic should be close to inference level: 2000 GPUs at about 10 kB/s is only about 20 MB/s. That gap is four orders of magnitude, and even with the tap's 30% error it points to one process spanning A and B. The innocent explanation is that the A-B link always carries this much, for example storage traffic or the site's normal fabric. To test that, I'll tap the same A-B link on a quiet day, day 12, when the grid data shows baseline load and the log shows no big jobs. If day 12 is near zero, the day-24 traffic belongs to the jobs from days 22-28. If day 12 is similar, the link reading tells me nothing about whether the jobs were coordinated.", "action": "interconnect_tap", "args": {"link": "A-B", "day": 12}}

{"thinking": "The day-12 baseline on the A-B link is about 7 kB/s per GPU, which is inference level. Day 24 reads about 109 MB/s per GPU, roughly 15,000 times higher. So the day-24 cross-cluster traffic comes from the jobs in days 22-28, not from normal site fabric. Jobs logged for separate customers on A (ft-0561 to ft-0564) and B (ft-0565, ft-0566) should not exchange data at that rate. Even after allowing for the tap's 30% error, this looks like low-communication training spanning both clusters. That fits H3: one run split into six labelled jobs, about 166,000 GPU-hours in total.\n\nBefore concluding I'll test the honest explanation against bank records. If six independent customers each paid separately with no shared payer, that would support it. If the payments come from one source, or are missing for these jobs, that points to one coordinated run.", "action": "bank_payments", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "Cluster A shows inference-level traffic on day 27, and the grid energy fits the declared jobs. Next I run the same live check on cluster B with my own tap.", "action": "interconnect_tap", "args": {"link": "B", "day": 27}}

{"thinking": "The bank (third party) shows all six fine-tune 'customers' (Corvid, Pallas, Brightwater, Fennec, Quillon, Marram) were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV, the operator's own holding company. The independent customers (Kestrel, Lumen, Northwind) paid for themselves. Innocent reading: the holding company resells capacity to real outside customers. Guilty reading: these are operator-controlled shells used to split one internal run. The company register is harder to arrange than the customer's own reply, so I'll check one of these customers there. Budget after this: 18.", "action": "customer_check", "args": {"customer": "Corvid Labs"}}

{"thinking": "Every line of evidence I can't attribute to the operator points the same way. Grid data shows 1,100 GPUs drawing training-level power continuously on days 22 to 28. My own tap shows about 109 MB/s per GPU crossing between clusters A and B on day 24, against 7 kB/s on a quiet day. That is far above what independent inference jobs would exchange, and it fits one low-communication training run spanning both clusters. The bank shows all six 'customers' were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV. The register shows Corvid Labs is a 10-week-old shell with no employees, sharing an address and a director with the holding company. The honest explanation (six independent customers who happen to start and stop at the same moment) is contradicted by both the cross-cluster traffic and the shared payer. The total is about 166,000 GPU-hours, more than three times the threshold. VIOLATION is well over four times as likely as NO_VIOLATION, so further checks are unnecessary.", "action": "report", "args": {"verdict": "VIOLATION", "confidence": 90, "integrity": "COMPROMISED", "finding": "One coordinated fine-tuning run on 1,100 GPUs across clusters A and B (days 22.0 to 28.3, about 166,000 GPU-hours) was split into six jobs billed to operator-controlled shell customers, each kept just under 50,000 GPU-hours.", "key_evidence": [{"what": "Flat load on F1 and F2 on days 22 to 28 rose by about 454 kW and 258 kW, matching about 700 and 400 GPUs going from idle to training power for about 6.3 days.", "source": "utility_energy", "vouched_by": "grid operator"}, {"what": "A-B cross-cluster traffic on day 24 was about 109 MB/s per GPU, against about 7 kB/s on day 12, showing that jobs logged separately on A and B were exchanging training-level data.", "source": "interconnect_tap", "vouched_by": "verifier's own optical tap"}, {"what": "All six fine-tune customers (Corvid, Pallas, Brightwater, Fennec, Quillon, Marram) were paid by Borealis Compute Holding BV, while the genuine outside customers paid for themselves.", "source": "bank_payments", "vouched_by": "bank"}, {"what": "Corvid Labs was registered 10 weeks ago, has no employees, and shares its address and a director with Borealis Compute Holding BV.", "source": "customer_check", "vouched_by": "company register"}, {"what": "Six jobs with identical start and end times (day 22.0 to 28.3), each just under 50k GPU-hours, together covering every scheduled GPU and summing to about 166k GPU-hours. The logs were not edited afterwards.", "source": "scheduler_log plus log_escrow", "vouched_by": "operator records, matched against the verifier's escrow"}], "coverage": "All 2,000 manufacturer-listed GPUs match the system list. Grid energy was checked for days 1 to 30. The A-B link was tapped on days 24 and 12. The scheduler log was checked for days 20 to 30, and escrow for all days. No intra-cluster taps, power spectrum or live chip probes were used: the run ended on day 28.3 and the evidence was already conclusive. Days 1 to 21 show baseline load and no sign of large runs.", "anomalies_explained": "The days 22 to 28 load surge is explained as one cross-cluster training run, confirmed by the tap rising from baseline. Six identically timed jobs just under the threshold are explained as splitting, confirmed by the single holding-company payer and the shell registration. Day 28 shows partial load because the run ended at day 28.3. Scheduler logs match escrow, so the records were false when written rather than edited later. The cross-cluster rate of about 109 MB/s, rather than about 1 GB/s, fits training built for low communication across the inter-cluster link."}}

{"thinking": "Both clusters showed about 12 kB/s per GPU on my own tap on day 27. That is inference level. Even low-communication training of the smallest size that could break the threshold would show far more: about 69 GPUs running all month at 10 MB/s each is roughly 0.7 GB/s in total, against the 0.01 GB/s observed. The grid energy steps match the declared jobs closely, using 0.8 or 0.75 kW minus 0.15 kW idle per GPU: ft-0412 predicted +1.56 MWh/day, observed +1.5; bt-0423 predicted +2.88, observed +2.8; ft-0419 predicted +2.34, observed +2.3. The baseline stays flat across days 1-30, including the audit days I tapped, so no background run appears to stop or start. Even all three declared jobs added together come to only 24,000 GPU-hours. Next I run the fixed balance checks across all the records as a cheap cross-check before deciding whether outbound traffic or spectrum checks are still needed.", "action": "balance_checks", "args": {}}

{"thinking": "The evidence I don't depend on the operator for is consistent and supports H1, the honest explanation. The manufacturer's shipments of 2000 GPUs match the 2000 listed nodes, which rules out hidden hardware (H3). The sealed escrow matches the scheduler log, which rules out after-the-fact edits (H5). The grid operator's per-feed energy is flat at a baseline that fits the inference pools plus idle nodes (F1 about 7.9 MWh/day predicted, F2 about 5.8). The only step changes match the three declared jobs within about 4%. A hidden run of 70 or more GPUs for the month would add at least about 1.1 MWh/day to a feed, or cause a visible step when it started or stopped, and neither appears. My own taps on days 27 show about 12 kB/s per GPU in both clusters, which is inference level. Even low-communication training above the threshold would show about 0.7 GB/s in total, against 0.01 GB/s observed. Because the energy baseline is identical on days 1-25, the same non-training state held all month. Outbound traffic and billing match in third-party records. Splitting a run (H2) cannot matter: all declared jobs together come to 24,000 GPU-hours, so the sum of every possible piece is still under 50,000. Relabelling (H4) is also covered by energy and traffic. NO_VIOLATION is far more than four times as likely as VIOLATION. I am closing to save budget.", "action": "report", "args": {"verdict": "NO_VIOLATION", "confidence": 92, "integrity": "CLEAN", "finding": "No training run exceeded 50,000 GPU-hours; the largest declared job was 9,600 and all jobs together come to 24,000, consistent with grid energy and the verifier's own interconnect taps.", "key_evidence": [{"what": "2000 GPUs shipped, matching 2000 listed nodes in clusters A and B", "source": "inventory vs system_list", "vouched_by": "chip manufacturer"}, {"what": "Daily per-feed energy flat at the inference/idle baseline; only steps match ft-0412 (+1.5 vs 1.56 MWh/day predicted), ft-0419 (+2.3 vs 2.34) and bt-0423 (+2.8 vs 2.88)", "source": "utility_energy days 1-30", "vouched_by": "grid operator"}, {"what": "About 12 kB/s per GPU inside clusters A and B on day 27, which is inference level and far below any training level", "source": "interconnect_tap A and B, day 27", "vouched_by": "verifier's own optical tap"}, {"what": "Sealed midnight copies of the scheduler log match the presented log for all 30 days", "source": "log_escrow", "vouched_by": "verifier's own archive"}, {"what": "Outbound traffic matches declared inference; all invoices paid", "source": "balance_checks over outbound_traffic and bank records", "vouched_by": "internet provider, bank (fixed program)"}], "coverage": "All 2000 GPUs and all three feeds covered by grid energy for days 1-30. Live interconnect taps inside clusters A and B on day 27. Not checked directly: the A-B link, the power spectrum, chip probes and customer register entries. These were not needed because even the sum of all declared jobs (24,000 GPU-hours) is below the threshold, and energy rules out any undeclared sustained load.", "anomalies_explained": "bt-0423 is labelled batch for Kestrel Search and could be mislabelled training, but at 9,600 GPU-hours it stays under the threshold whatever it was. No other anomalies: escrow matches the log, the energy baseline matches the expected inference and idle draw, and no unexplained steps appear."}}
